Bounding Fixed Points of Non-Monotone Processes: Theory to Practice

CCS: Theory of computation Constraint and logic programmingCCS: Theory of computation AbstractionCCS: Theory of computation Branch-and-boundCCS: Software and its engineering Formal software verification
Abdullah Rasheed email: arasheed@utexas.edu Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA and Vijay K. Garg email: garg@ece.utexas.edu Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas, USA
Abstract.

Many modern solvers and program analyzers rely on non-monotone reasoning (e.g. negation-as-failure, speculative updates, backtracking) for which classical monotone fixed-point methods do not apply. The general problem of finding the fixed points of these processes is a difficult one. For this reason, there have been theoretical efforts in existing Approximation Fixpoint Theory (AFT) from the domain of logic programming to approximate fixed points of non-monotone operators. Tight approximations of these fixed points are highly useful for accelerating non-monotonic computations by restricting the search space. In practice, however, even the best approximations obtained through AFT can be coarse and computationally expensive. We aim to address both issues to make AFT approximation methods practical for use in programming languages (PL) settings. To mitigate inefficiency, we prove the soundness of an abstract interpretation for approximating operators. To improve upon coarse approximations, we carefully introduce controlled unsoundness to design an effective yet practical algorithm for partitioning and tightening AFT’s best approximations. This algorithm is sound, anytime, and guarantees termination on finite-height lattices. We further present a modification that ensures polynomial-time complexity. We instantiate these methods in two settings: (1) answer set programming, where it serves as a convergence-accelerating pre-processor, and (2) speculative program analysis, where it reduces rollback while preserving soundness. In both settings, we focus on implementation-level details to demonstrate the practical applicability of our methods.

Keywords: 
Non-monotonic fixed-point approximation, Iterative refinement, Speculative processes, Answer set programming

1. Introduction

Many analyses and algorithms in programming languages are designed around monotonic computation. Monotonicity provides a well-understood foundation: once a fact is derived, it remains true, and states evolve along a chain S1⊑S2⊑⋯S_{1}\sqsubseteq S_{2}\sqsubseteq\cdots that reaches a fixed point. This property underlies a vast range of techniques from dataflow analysis and abstract interpretation to type inference and constraint solving. However, monotonicity also comes at a cost: once a decision is made, it cannot be retracted. This rigidity limits the ability of such systems to model speculative reasoning or reversible computation, both of which are increasingly common in modern algorithms and implementations.

In contrast, non-monotonic processes allow information to be withdrawn or revised. Such behavior arises naturally in domains that rely on backtracking, revision, or speculation. For example, the decision process of Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL) SAT solvers backtracks when a decision leads to a conflict (marques2009); speculative optimizations in dynamic compilers and program analyses assume properties that may later be invalidated (holzle1992; fluckiger2017; devecsery2018); and non-monotonic reasoning forms the basis of Answer Set Programming (ASP) which is widely utilized in knowledge representation and has been used in program analysis, model checking, constraint solving, and much more (marek1997; erdem2016; heljanko2003; dawson1996). These examples demonstrate that, in practical applications, non-monotonicity is not a defect to be avoided but a powerful mechanism for adaptability and efficiency.

Speculative program analyses are modeled in this paper as a concrete instance of non-monotonic behavior. Such analyses often assume facts that may later be invalidated as new information becomes available, forcing them to retract or revise earlier speculations. We demonstrate that there exists a non-monotone (in fact, anti-monotone) operator whose fixed points coincide exactly with the sets of “stable” assumptions. That is, an operator Φ\Phi that makes necessary revisions to the set of assumptions σ\sigma and whose fixed points σ=Φ⁡(σ)\sigma=\Phi(\sigma) are the sets that are not refuted in the speculative analysis computed by assuming σ\sigma. Furthermore, with a larger set of assumptions, a more precise analysis is computed, which in turn can disprove more assumptions. It is then evident that Φ\Phi is non-monotone (in fact, anti-monotone). Identifying these stable sets of assumptions enables analyses to improve precision and optimize performance. For instance, a dynamic analysis can apply a given set of stable assumptions to reduce unnecessary retractions or deoptimizations caused by runtime counter-examples.

Despite its practical relevance, the approximation of fixed points of non-monotone functions has received little attention in programming languages. Existing approaches rely heavily on monotonicity to guarantee convergence and soundness, while non-monotonicity is often feared for its lack thereof. This paper bridges that gap by taking advantage of existing theory and introducing new results to present practical and effective approaches for approximating the fixed points of non-monotone functions in PL settings while improving upon theoretical barriers.

Contributions

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    AFT with Abstractions. We prove a new soundness theorem for abstract interpretation of non-monotone fixed point approximation, enabling quicker computation of AFT operators abstractly.

  • •

    Branch-and-Bound Approximations. We devise an effective anytime branch-and-bound style algorithm that often produces a set of tighter approximations than AFT prescribes. In particular, it finds a set of approximations that spans all fixed points such that the total size of all bounds is bounded from above by the size of the best possible approximation guaranteed by AFT. We establish termination (for finite height lattices) and soundness guarantees while retaining practical efficiency by leveraging structural properties of a generalized AFT operator to prune the search space. We also introduce modifications that guarantee polynomial time complexity in the height of the lattice (when the lattice is finite height and the approximation refinement is efficient, enabled by lattice abstractions, structural properties of the given function, or a restricted refinement).

  • •

    Feasibility and Demonstration in PL Practice. We model speculative program analysis in this paradigm, showing that the approach integrates cleanly in PL settings and the algorithms deliver tangible benefits, thereby evidencing practical feasibility for such tasks. We focus on implementation-level details, outlining the trade-offs with integration, and the use cases where these methods are most effective.

  • •

    Use Case for Pre-Processing. We demonstrate, using the example of ASP solving, how our methods can be used as a pre-processing step for problem domains in our paradigm by substantially reducing the search space size, thereby improving efficiency. We again focus on implementation-level details and illustrate how our proposed algorithm can reduce the workload of existing ASP solvers.

2. Related Work

The study of approximating fixed points of non-monotone operators is not a new one. In fact, an Approximation Fixpoint Theory (AFT) was proposed long ago for the purposes of analyzing, defining, and approximating semantics of non-monotone logics (denecker2000). Since its introduction, the theory has continued to develop and find use in the areas of knowledge representation and logic programming (denecker2012; strass2013; liu2022). AFT is an algebraic framework for the approximation of fixed points using “approximation operators” over a bilattice of pairs, with the property that they bound the fixed points of the original, possibly non-monotone function in an interval. In (denecker2004), the notion of an “ultimate approximation” is introduced as a necessarily existing unique and most precise (partial) approximation. Despite being the best approximation, it may still a coarse one (possibly even spanning the entire lattice). In this paper, we restate the ultimate approximation in a more concrete and compact manner, demonstrate its soundness for approximating subsets of fixed points in subspaces, and crucially, take advantage of these properties to design an algorithm that improves the bound beyond the ultimate approximation.

AFT originated in the world of knowledge representation, and has been applied to the stable model and well-founded semantics of logic programs (denecker2004; denecker2000; gelfond1988; gelder1991). We further extend this example by applying our branch-and-bound style heuristic to narrow in on even tighter approximations for stable models in logic programs. Furthermore, we take a closer look at the implementation level details to see how our methods can serve as a pre-processor for speeding up ASP solvers. The work done in (eiter2004) particularly enables the integration of these methods by providing equivalence guarantees under specific “partial evaluations” of a logic program.

To bridge this theory from the domain of knowledge representation to the practice of programming languages, we show that program analysis is a suitable use-case. Furthermore, we revisit the optimistic hybrid analysis proposed in (devecsery2018). Their approach infers a set of “likely invariants” from a sample of executions. These likely invariants are then fed as assumptions to a static analyzer to produce an unsound yet more precise analysis whose assumptions are later verified dynamically. However, as outlined in their paper, when those assumptions fail, the runtime system bears the cost. Optimizations are rolled back and the program must re-execute. We formalize the problem of finding a consistent assumption set by showing that it reduces to finding fixed points of a non-monotone operator. Depending on the application, these stable sets can represent assumptions that are not provably inconsistent or those provably consistent under speculative analysis. Our heuristic can be used to help effectively identify such stable sets, reducing dynamic rollback and improving predictability.

3. Background

A partially ordered set (L,≤)(L,\leq) is a complete lattice if every subset S⊆LS\subseteq L has both a least upper bound (supremum, or join, denoted ⨆S\bigsqcup S) and a greatest lower bound (infimum, or meet, denoted ⨅S\bigsqcap S). Every complete lattice has a top element (⊤=⨆L\top=\bigsqcup L) and a bottom element (⊥=⨅L\bot=\bigsqcap L). We also use sup\sup and inf\inf to represent ⨆\bigsqcup and ⨅\bigsqcap respectively. Two elements x,y∈Lx,y\in L are incomparable if x≰yx\nleq y and y≰xy\nleq x. This is denoted by x||yx||y. The height of a lattice is ℓ(L)=sup{k∣⊥L=x0≤⋯≤xk=⊤L}\ell(L)=\sup\{k\mid\bot_{L}=x_{0}\leq\cdots\leq x_{k}=\top_{L}\}. If ℓ⁡(L)\ell(L) is not defined, then we may write ℓ⁡(L)=∞\ell(L)=\infty.

Given two posets (P,≤P)(P,\leq_{P}) and (Q,≤Q)(Q,\leq_{Q}), a function f:P→Qf:P\to Q is monotone (or order-preserving) if for all x,y∈Px,y\in P, x≤Pyx\leq_{P}y implies f(x)≤Qf(y)f(x)\leq_{Q}f(y). On the other hand, ff is anti-monotone if for all x,y∈Px,y\in P, x≤Pyx\leq_{P}y implies f(x)≥Qf(y)f(x)\geq_{Q}f(y).

Theorem 3.1 (Knaster-Tarski Fixed-Point Theorem).

Let (L,≤)(L,\leq) be a complete lattice and f:L→Lf:L\to L be a monotone function. The set of fixed points of ff in LL is a non-empty complete lattice. It contains a least fixed point lfp⁡(f)\operatorname{lfp}(f) and a greatest fixed point gfp⁡(f)\operatorname{gfp}(f), given by:

lfp⁡(f)=⨅{x∈L∣f⁡(x)≤x}\operatorname{lfp}(f)=\bigsqcap\{x\in L\mid f(x)\leq x\}
gfp⁡(f)=⨆{x∈L∣x≤f⁡(x)}\operatorname{gfp}(f)=\bigsqcup\{x\in L\mid x\leq f(x)\}

An element x∈Lx\in L is called a pre-fixed point if f⁡(x)≤xf(x)\leq x, and it is called a post-fixed point if x≤f⁡(x)x\leq f(x). Then, lfp⁡(f)\operatorname{lfp}(f) is the infimum of the pre-fixed points and gfp⁡(f)\operatorname{gfp}(f) is the supremum of the post-fixed point when ff is monotone. We will denote the set of fixed points of ff by Fix⁡(f)={x∈L∣x=f⁡(x)}\operatorname{Fix}(f)=\{x\in L\mid x=f(x)\}.

A chain is a subset S⊆LS\subseteq L such that for all x,y∈Sx,y\in S, x≤yx\leq y or y≤xy\leq x. A chain {xk}\{x_{k}\} is ascending if x1≤x2≤…x_{1}\leq x_{2}\leq\ldots, and it is descending if x1≥x2≥…x_{1}\geq x_{2}\geq\ldots.

An ascending or descending chain {xk}\{x_{k}\} stabilizes if there is some jj such that xj=xj+1=…x_{j}=x_{j+1}=\ldots. A lattice LL satisfies the Ascending Chain Condition (ACC) if every ascending chain stabilizes, and it satisfies the Descending Chain Condition if every descending chain stabilizes.

Let CC and AA be complete lattices. Then, if α:C→A\alpha:C\to A and γ:A→C\gamma:A\to C are monotone, α⊣γ\alpha\dashv\gamma iff α(x)≤Ay⇔x≤Cγ(y)\alpha(x)\leq_{A}y\Leftrightarrow x\leq_{C}\gamma(y) (α\alpha is called the left-adjoint and γ\gamma is called the right-adjoint). This pair of functions forms a Galois connection. It is necessarily true that α\alpha preserves arbitrary joins and γ\gamma preserves arbitrary meets. If α​γ=idA\alpha\gamma=\mathrm{id}_{A} (equivalently, α\alpha is surjective, and also equivalently, γ\gamma is injective), then they form a Galois insertion.

3.1. Answer Set Programming

A (logic) program PP is a set of rules of the form

A←L1,…,LmA\leftarrow L_{1},\ldots,L_{m}

where AA is an atom and each LiL_{i} is a literal (either a positive or a negative atom). The rule states, in an informal sense, that if L1,…,LmL_{1},\ldots,L_{m} hold, then AA should also hold in a given interpretation of the ground atoms. A program PP is non-stratified if it has recursion through negation (the exact definition will not be important in this paper). These programs are provably harder than stratified ones, and their main reasoning tasks are NP/coNP-complete (eiter1995; marek1999). The Herbrand base HPH_{P} of PP is the set of all ground atoms occuring in PP (after grounding all variables), and an Herbrand model MM of PP is a subset of the Herbrand base such that setting the atoms of MM to true (and everything else to false; two-valued logic) satisfies the rules of PP. For example, in the program

a\displaystyle a ←\displaystyle\leftarrow
b\displaystyle b ←a,c\displaystyle\leftarrow a,c

the Herbrand base is {a,b,c}\{a,b,c\} and the Herbrand models are {a},{a,b},{a,b,c}\{a\},\{a,b\},\{a,b,c\}. Observe that {}\{\} is not an Herbrand model because the rule a←a\leftarrow requires every Herbrand model to contain aa. Also, {a,c}\{a,c\} is not an Herbrand model because the rule b←a,cb\leftarrow a,c states that, since we have a,ca,c, we should also have bb.

An Herbrand model MM is minimal if no strict subset of MM is an Herbrand model.

Given any subset MM of the Herbrand base, the Gelfond-Lifschitz reduction PMP_{M} of the program PP is as follows:

  1. (1)

    for all A∈MA\in M, remove all rules that contain AA negatively in the body (i.e. any rule of the form B←…,¬A,…B\leftarrow\ldots,\neg A,\ldots).

  2. (2)

    remove all negative literals in the bodies of all rules of PP

The reduct PMP_{M} is always a positive program. That is, it contains no negative literals and thus has a unique minimal Herbrand model. The unique minimal Herbrand model of a positive program can be found by repeatedly applying the rules of the program to the empty set until a fixed point is reached. The unique minimal Herbrand model of PMP_{M} is denoted by SP​(M)S_{P}(M). We call SPS_{P} the Gelfond-Lifschitz (GL) operator (parameterized by PP). Note that SPS_{P} is anti-monotone since for larger MM, the reduct PMP_{M} is smaller.

A subset MM of the Herbrand base is called a stable model (or answer set) of PP if the unique minimal Herbrand model of PMP_{M} is equal to MM (it is a fixed point of SPS_{P}). Stable models are “self-supporting,” and are of great importance in answer set programming. For example, when modeling combinatorial optimization problems, stable models often correspond to minimal solutions. This is shown in the following theorem.

Theorem 3.2.

Any stable model of PP is a minimal Herbrand model of PP (gelfond1988).

4. Initial Monotone Approximations

To approximate the fixed points of a (possibly) non-monotone operator, we approximate it from above and below. In particular, we approximate it using monotone envelopes for ease of computation. This is effectively a more concrete and digestible restatement of the ultimate approximation (denecker2004). The discussion in this section is valuable, but generalization begins at Section 5 and results needed for our later algorithm subsequently follow.

For a given function, we are interested in the least monotone over-approximation. This will allow us to use a monotone approximating function to find an initial approximation that will be refined. Let LL be a complete lattice and f:L→Lf:L\to L. We then define

fu​(x)=supy≤xf⁡(y)f^{u}(x)=\sup_{y\leq x}f(y)

and observe that fuf^{u} is the pointwise least (the best) monotone function over-approximating ff (cousot1979). Our eventual goal will be to iteratively restrict the domain for which fuf^{u} is monotone to improve the approximation.

To do this, we also utilize a best monotone under-approximation of ff. Define fℓf^{\ell} as

fℓ​(x)=infy≥xf⁡(y)f^{\ell}(x)=\inf_{y\geq x}f(y)

and observe the dual property that fℓf^{\ell} is the greatest (the best) monotone under-approximation of ff. These envelopes fℓ,fuf^{\ell},f^{u} correspond to the lower/upper borders of AFT’s ultimate approximation. To approximate solutions to x=f⁡(x)x=f(x), these approximations will work dually together to improve each other’s approximation by restricting the domain over which the other function needs to be monotone. For the sake of simplicity throughout this paper, we will assume that ff indeed has a fixed point.

We now have best upper and lower bound monotone functions fu,fℓf^{u},f^{\ell} for ff. For the purposes of fixed point computation/approximation, there are a variety of methods known for monotone functions. We will use the easier problem of finding the least fixed point and greatest fixed point of monotone functions (namely, fuf^{u} and fℓf^{\ell}) to approximate the fixed points of the non-monotone function ff. As we will soon see, this approximation will be a bound containing all fixed points of ff (given they exist). This final bound provides a restricted search space for the fixed points of ff along with a verifiable certificate of “closeness” to a fixed point.

Also observe that, at face value, computing fuf^{u} and fℓf^{\ell} is computationally infeasible. It may require taking the supremum/infimum over a very large subset, which can be just as expensive to compute as a brute force search. In the examples presented throughout this paper, we observe that in many scenarios (when the envelopes have closed-form solutions), these approximating monotone functions are much more computationally feasible than they initially seem. Anti-monotone functions will later be of particular interest. To remedy the cases that the approximating functions are not computationally feasible, we later prove that an abstract interpretation can be induced for the approximation operator while maintaining soundness in the resulting bounds.

Example 4.1.

Throughout this paper, we will demonstrate the refinement process on a non-monotone function ff that represents the “best response” of two actors in a system. The fixed points of this function can be thought of as the Nash Equilibrium of a game with two players.

Let L=[0,1]×[0,1]L=[0,1]\times[0,1] ordered component-wise, and let

f⁡(x1,x2)=(B​R1​(x2),B​R2​(x1))f(x_{1},x_{2})=(BR_{1}(x_{2}),BR_{2}(x_{1}))

be a function where x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} are the current fractions of resources that player 1 and player 2 have claimed respectively. The “best response” of player 1 is B​R1​(x2)=1−x22BR_{1}(x_{2})=1-x_{2}^{2} (if player 2 takes more resources, player 1 takes quadratically less). The “best response” of player 2 is B​R2​(x1)=x1/2BR_{2}(x_{1})=x_{1}/2 (if player 1 claims more resources, player 2 claims a fraction of them).

Observe that ff is non-monotone: (0.5,0.5)≤(1,1)(0.5,0.5)\leq(1,1) but f⁡(0.5,0.5)=(0.75,0.25)f(0.5,0.5)=(0.75,0.25) and f⁡(1,1)=(0,0.5)f(1,1)=(0,0.5). To simplify the approximating monotone functions, first observe that f⁡(x1,x2)f(x_{1},x_{2}) is maximized when x2x_{2} is minimized and x1x_{1} is maximized. Then, the over-approximating monotone function simplifies to

fu​(x1,x2)=sup(y1,y2)≤(x1,x2)f⁡(y1,y2)=f⁡(x1,0)f^{u}(x_{1},x_{2})=\sup_{(y_{1},y_{2})\leq(x_{1},x_{2})}f(y_{1},y_{2})=f(x_{1},0)

For the under-approximating function, observe that f⁡(x1,x2)f(x_{1},x_{2}) is minimized when x2x_{2} is maximized and x1x_{1} is minimized. Then the under-approximating monotone function simplifies to

fℓ​(x1,x2)=inf(x1,x2)≤(y1,y2)f⁡(y1,y2)=f⁡(x1,1)f^{\ell}(x_{1},x_{2})=\inf_{(x_{1},x_{2})\leq(y_{1},y_{2})}f(y_{1},y_{2})=f(x_{1},1)

To obtain a safe bound on the fixed points, we progress the upper and lower bound cautiously by finding safe solutions to x≤fu​(x)x\leq f^{u}(x) and x≥fℓ​(x)x\geq f^{\ell}(x). Since fuf^{u} and fℓf^{\ell} are monotone, they have a greatest/least solution to their respective problems by the lattice’s partial-order unlike ff. In particular, the safest (greatest) solution to x≤fu​(x)x\leq f^{u}(x) is

⨆{x∈L∣x≤fu​(x)}=gfp⁡(fu)\bigsqcup\{x\in L\mid x\leq f^{u}(x)\}=\operatorname{gfp}(f^{u})

by the Knaster-Tarski fixed point theorem. The dual holds for fℓf^{\ell}. Let

xu\displaystyle x^{u} =gfp⁡(fu)\displaystyle=\operatorname{gfp}(f^{u})
xℓ\displaystyle x^{\ell} =lfp⁡(fℓ)\displaystyle=\operatorname{lfp}(f^{\ell})
Theorem 4.2.

For all fixed points μ\mu of ff, xℓ≤μ≤xux^{\ell}\leq\mu\leq x^{u}.

Proof.

Let μ\mu be a fixed point of ff. Then μ=f⁡(μ)≤fu​(μ)\mu=f(\mu)\leq f^{u}(\mu), so μ≤xu\mu\leq x^{u} by Knaster-Tarski. Similarly, μ=f⁡(μ)≥fℓ​(μ)\mu=f(\mu)\geq f^{\ell}(\mu), so xℓ≤μx^{\ell}\leq\mu by Knaster-Tarski. ∎

Indeed, these are the best achievable bounds in the sense that they are the tightest bounds obtainable by the tightest sound interval transformer for ff (denecker2004). Namely, [xℓ,xu][x^{\ell},x^{u}] is AFT’s well-founded approximation for ff.

Example 4.3.

We pick up where we left off in Example 4.1. By applying Kleene iteration on fuf^{u} and fℓf^{\ell}, we find their greatest and least fixed points respectively.

fu​(1,1)\displaystyle f^{u}(1,1) =f⁡(1,0)=(1,0.5)\displaystyle=f(1,0)=(1,0.5)
fu​(1,0.5)\displaystyle f^{u}(1,0.5) =f⁡(1,0)=(1,0.5)\displaystyle=f(1,0)=(1,0.5)

so xu=(1,0.5)x^{u}=(1,0.5). To find xℓx^{\ell}, we apply Kleene iteration on fℓf^{\ell}:

fℓ​(0,0)=f⁡(0,1)=(0,0)\displaystyle f^{\ell}(0,0)=f(0,1)=(0,0)

so xℓ=(0,0)x^{\ell}=(0,0). We have reached the initial bound

(0,0)≤μ≤(1,0.5)(0,0)\leq\mu\leq(1,0.5)

and as we shall soon see, this bound can be improved by refining fuf^{u} and fℓf^{\ell}.

5. Iterative Approximation Refinement

We can view an iterative refinement of the monotone envelopes as repeated application of a “refinement” function. That is, a function FF over intervals (or bounds; they will be used interchangeably) such that

F⁡([xk−1ℓ,xk−1u])=[xkℓ,xku]F([x_{k-1}^{\ell},x_{k-1}^{u}])=[x_{k}^{\ell},x_{k}^{u}]

We can generalize this function to the set of all intervals, not just those generated by [⊥,⊤][\bot,\top] to show a useful result that states that if we begin at an arbitrary bound approximating an optimal solution, then we will stay in a sound state after repeated application of FF.

We first define the function FF to be a function over the set of bounds 𝔅={[xℓ,xu]∣xℓ,xu∈L∧xℓ≤xu}\mathfrak{B}=\{[x^{\ell},x^{u}]\mid x^{\ell},x^{u}\in L\wedge x^{\ell}\leq x^{u}\} to be

F⁡(B)=[lfpB⁡(fBℓ),gfpB⁡(fBu)]F(B)=[\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f_{B}^{\ell}),\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(f_{B}^{u})]

where fBℓf_{B}^{\ell} and fBuf_{B}^{u} are defined by

fBℓ​(x)\displaystyle f_{B}^{\ell}(x) =infx≤y≤xuf⁡(y)\displaystyle=\inf_{x\leq y\leq x^{u}}f(y)
fBu​(x)\displaystyle f_{B}^{u}(x) =supxℓ≤y≤xf⁡(y)\displaystyle=\sup_{x^{\ell}\leq y\leq x}f(y)

and

lfpB⁡(g)\displaystyle\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(g) =⨅{x∈L∣x≥xℓ∧x≥g⁡(x)}\displaystyle=\bigsqcap\{x\in L\mid x\geq x^{\ell}\land x\geq g(x)\}
gfpB⁡(g)\displaystyle\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(g) =⨆{x∈L∣x≤xu∧x≤g⁡(x)}\displaystyle=\bigsqcup\{x\in L\mid x\leq x^{u}\land x\leq g(x)\}

are the Knaster-Tarski least/greatest fixed point definitions over a restricted domain. We emphasize that the meet and join is in the lattice LL, rather the interval’s sub-lattice meet/join (for the cases of empty sets). Observe that fBℓf^{\ell}_{B} and fBuf^{u}_{B} are monotone over BB. They are a generalization of the earlier monotone envelopes. It is not hard to show that for the monotone functions φBℓ​(x)=xℓ⊔fBℓ​(x)\varphi^{\ell}_{B}(x)=x^{\ell}\sqcup f^{\ell}_{B}(x) and φBu​(x)=xu⊓fBu​(x)\varphi^{u}_{B}(x)=x^{u}\sqcap f^{u}_{B}(x), lfp⁡(φBℓ)=lfpB⁡(fBℓ)\operatorname{lfp}(\varphi^{\ell}_{B})=\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f^{\ell}_{B}) and gfp⁡(φBu)=gfpB⁡(fBu)\operatorname{gfp}(\varphi^{u}_{B})=\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(f^{u}_{B}). Thus computing lfpB⁡(fBℓ)\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f^{\ell}_{B}) and gfpB⁡(fBu)\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(f^{u}_{B}) reduces to computing the least/greatest fixed point of monotone functions.

Example 5.1.

Building on Examples 4.1 and 4.3, we define the refined functions f2uf_{2}^{u} and f2ℓf_{2}^{\ell} (fBuf^{u}_{B} and fBℓf^{\ell}_{B} for B=[x1ℓ,x1u]B=[x^{\ell}_{1},x^{u}_{1}]). In Example 4.3 we determined that x1u=(1,0.5)x_{1}^{u}=(1,0.5) and x1ℓ=(0,0)x_{1}^{\ell}=(0,0). This gives

f2u​(x1,x2)\displaystyle f_{2}^{u}(x_{1},x_{2}) =sup(0,0)≤(y1,y2)≤(x1,x2)f⁡(y1,y2)=f⁡(x1,0)\displaystyle=\sup_{(0,0)\leq(y_{1},y_{2})\leq(x_{1},x_{2})}f(y_{1},y_{2})=f(x_{1},0)
f2ℓ​(x1,x2)\displaystyle f_{2}^{\ell}(x_{1},x_{2}) =inf(x1,x2)≤(y1,y2)≤(1,0.5)f⁡(y1,y2)=f⁡(x1,0.5)\displaystyle=\inf_{(x_{1},x_{2})\leq(y_{1},y_{2})\leq(1,0.5)}f(y_{1},y_{2})=f(x_{1},0.5)

Here we observe that f2uf_{2}^{u} didn’t improve upon f1uf_{1}^{u} since x1ℓx_{1}^{\ell} didn’t improve upon x0ℓx_{0}^{\ell}. On the other hand, the dual approximation f2ℓf_{2}^{\ell} improved since x1ux_{1}^{u} improved upon x0ux_{0}^{u}.

We can now look for x2ux_{2}^{u} and x2ℓx_{2}^{\ell} given the definitions of f2uf_{2}^{u} and f2ℓf_{2}^{\ell}. The least/greatest fixed points can be found by using Kleene iteration on φ2ℓ\varphi^{\ell}_{2} and φ2u\varphi^{u}_{2} as described earlier, but in this example the result is no different. Since f2u=f1uf_{2}^{u}=f_{1}^{u}, we have x2u=x1u=(1,0.5)x_{2}^{u}=x_{1}^{u}=(1,0.5). For f2ℓf_{2}^{\ell} we find:

f2ℓ​(0,0)\displaystyle f_{2}^{\ell}(0,0) =f⁡(0,0.5)=(0.75,0)\displaystyle=f(0,0.5)=(0.75,0)
f2ℓ​(0.75,0)\displaystyle f_{2}^{\ell}(0.75,0) =f⁡(0.75,0.5)=(0.75,0.375)\displaystyle=f(0.75,0.5)=(0.75,0.375)
f2ℓ​(0.75,0.375)\displaystyle f_{2}^{\ell}(0.75,0.375) =f⁡(0.75,0.5)=(0.75,0.375)\displaystyle=f(0.75,0.5)=(0.75,0.375)

and we see that the lower bound x1ℓ=(0,0)x_{1}^{\ell}=(0,0) has been improved to x2ℓ=(0.75,0.375)x_{2}^{\ell}=(0.75,0.375). This improvement was a result of the dual bound x1ux_{1}^{u} tightening the domain of f2ℓf_{2}^{\ell}. Alas, we now see that our approximating bound for the fixed point has improved to

(0.75,0.375)≤μ≤(1,0.5)(0.75,0.375)\leq\mu\leq(1,0.5)

In terms of AFT, FF is comparable to the stable operator for the ultimate approximation (which we will call the DMT operator after Denecker, Marek, and Truszczyński) (denecker2004) with a small change: FF can map a valid bound to an invalid bound (not in 𝔅\mathfrak{B}). This difference comes from the fact that the stable operator (denecker2004) takes the least/greatest fixed point of the monotone envelopes over the whole domain, while we decide to restrict the domain. At first glance, this change seems harmful since it takes away some of the nice properties enjoyed in AFT. We do this intentionally to introduce potentially bad behavior when there is no fixed point in the interval. This will allow us to sometimes determine when an interval is unsound, which will be useful for the pruning step of our later algorithm.

In particular, it is not always the case that F⁡(B)∈𝔅F(B)\in\mathfrak{B} for an interval B∈𝔅B\in\mathfrak{B}. With the definition of FF, this is only guaranteed to hold for some intervals. As motivated earlier, we are interested in bounds that are sound in the same sense as we saw before.

Definition 5.2.

A bound B∈𝔅B\in\mathfrak{B} is sound (for ff) if it contains any μ∈Fix⁡(f)\mu\in\operatorname{Fix}(f).

This definition states that a bound is sound if it contains some solution. As we will see, this keeps the solution contained after each iteration. We first ensure that F⁡(B)F(B) is indeed sound and contained in 𝔅\mathfrak{B} for all sound B∈𝔅B\in\mathfrak{B}. For convenience, we will let 𝔅s​o​u​n​d={B∈𝔅∣B is sound}\mathfrak{B}_{sound}=\{B\in\mathfrak{B}\mid\text{$B$ is sound}\}.

Lemma 5.3.

For all B∈𝔅s​o​u​n​dB\in\mathfrak{B}_{sound}, F⁡(B)∈𝔅s​o​u​n​dF(B)\in\mathfrak{B}_{sound}.

Proof.

Since BB is sound, there exists a fixed point μ∈B\mu\in B of ff. Observe that μ=f⁡(μ)≤fBu​(μ)\mu=f(\mu)\leq f^{u}_{B}(\mu) and μ=f⁡(μ)≥fBℓ​(μ)\mu=f(\mu)\geq f^{\ell}_{B}(\mu) since μ∈B\mu\in B (and fBℓ≤f≤fBuf^{\ell}_{B}\leq f\leq f^{u}_{B} over BB), so lfpB⁡(fBℓ)≤μ≤gfpB⁡(fBu)\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f^{\ell}_{B})\leq\mu\leq\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(f^{u}_{B}) by definition. ∎

We now show that FF can only shrink bounds (provided they are sound), and directly after we show that if a bound is a sound approximation of any optimal solution, then it remains a sound approximation after applying FF.

Lemma 5.4.

For all B∈𝔅s​o​u​n​dB\in\mathfrak{B}_{sound}, F⁡(B)⊆BF(B)\subseteq B.

Proof.

Let B=[xℓ,xu]B=[x^{\ell},x^{u}]. It then suffices to show that lfpB⁡(fBℓ)≥xℓ\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f^{\ell}_{B})\geq x^{\ell} and gfpB⁡(fBu)≤xu\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(f^{u}_{B})\leq x^{u}. Since BB is sound, lfpB⁡(fBℓ)\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f^{\ell}_{B}) is a meet of a non-empty set of elements with xℓx^{\ell} as a lower bound, so xℓ≤lfpB⁡(fBℓ)x^{\ell}\leq\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f^{\ell}_{B}). A dual argument follows to show gfpB⁡(fBu)≤xu\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(f^{u}_{B})\leq x^{u}. ∎

These two lemmas will serve to be very useful in Section 6. To illustrate how Lemma 5.3 can be useful, the following example shows that if a bound is not sound, applying FF may take it to an invalid interval.

Example 5.5.

Consider the function ff from Example 4.1, starting from the bound B=[(0,0),(0.2,0.2)]B=[(0,0),(0.2,0.2)], which contains no fixed points. Applying FF on this bound gives

F⁡([(0,0),(0.2,0.2)])=[lfp⁡(φBℓ),gfp⁡(φBu)]F([(0,0),(0.2,0.2)])=[\operatorname{lfp}(\varphi^{\ell}_{B}),\operatorname{gfp}(\varphi^{u}_{B})]

and Kleene iteration on these functions gives lfp⁡(φBℓ)=(1,1)\operatorname{lfp}(\varphi^{\ell}_{B})=(1,1) and gfp⁡(φBu)=(0.2,0.1)\operatorname{gfp}(\varphi^{u}_{B})=(0.2,0.1), and [(1,1),(0.2,0.1)]∉𝔅[(1,1),(0.2,0.1)]\notin\mathfrak{B}, so by Lemma 5.3 it is necessarily true that there are no fixed points in [(0,0),(0.2,0.2)][(0,0),(0.2,0.2)].

Lemma 5.6.

For all B∈𝔅B\in\mathfrak{B}, if F⁡(B)∈𝔅F(B)\in\mathfrak{B} then F⁡(B)⊆BF(B)\subseteq B.

Proof.

Let B=[xℓ,xu]B=[x^{\ell},x^{u}] and observe that xℓx^{\ell} is a lower bound for lfpB⁡(fBℓ)\operatorname{lfp}_{B}(f^{\ell}_{B}) (even if it is a meet of an empty set) and xux^{u} is an upper bound for gfpB⁡(fBu)\operatorname{gfp}_{B}(f^{u}_{B}) (even if it is a join of an empty set), so F⁡(B)⊆BF(B)\subseteq B. ∎

Lemma 5.7.

If B1,B2∈𝔅s​o​u​n​dB_{1},B_{2}\in\mathfrak{B}_{sound} and B1⊆B2B_{1}\subseteq B_{2}, then F⁡(B1)⊆F⁡(B2)F(B_{1})\subseteq F(B_{2}).

Proof.

Let B1,B2∈𝔅B_{1},B_{2}\in\mathfrak{B} such that B1⊆B2B_{1}\subseteq B_{2} and let x∈B1x\in B_{1} such that x≥fB1ℓ​(x)x\geq f^{\ell}_{B_{1}}(x) (existence guaranteed by soundness of B1B_{1}). Then, since B1⊆B2B_{1}\subseteq B_{2}, fB1ℓ≥fB2ℓf^{\ell}_{B_{1}}\geq f^{\ell}_{B_{2}} over B1B_{1} (meet of a smaller set of elements is larger), so

x≥fB1ℓ​(x)≥fB2ℓ​(x)x\geq f^{\ell}_{B_{1}}(x)\geq f^{\ell}_{B_{2}}(x)

and the set of pre-fixed points of B1B_{1} is a subset of the set of pre-fixed points of B2B_{2}. Thus,

lfpB1⁡(fB1ℓ)≥lfpB2⁡(fB2ℓ)\operatorname{lfp}_{B_{1}}(f^{\ell}_{B_{1}})\geq\operatorname{lfp}_{B_{2}}(f^{\ell}_{B_{2}})

Dually, we observe that gfpB1⁡(fB1u)≤gfpB2⁡(fB2u)\operatorname{gfp}_{B_{1}}(f^{u}_{B_{1}})\leq\operatorname{gfp}_{B_{2}}(f^{u}_{B_{2}}) holds. Finally, this shows that F⁡(B1)⊆F⁡(B2)F(B_{1})\subseteq F(B_{2}). ∎

The following theorem essentially restates known monotone iteration convergence results. We state the theorem to emphasize that by starting at a bound that is not generated by {Fk​([⊥,⊤])}\{F^{k}([\bot,\top])\}, we do not end in a bound worse than X∞=infk≥0Fk​([⊥,⊤])X_{\infty}=\inf_{k\geq 0}F^{k}([\bot,\top]) (the bound approached by starting at the interval of the entire lattice).

Theorem 5.8.

Let B∈𝔅s​o​u​n​dB\in\mathfrak{B}_{sound} and let B∞=infk≥0Fk​(B)B_{\infty}=\inf_{k\geq 0}F^{k}(B). Then, B∞⊆X∞B_{\infty}\subseteq X_{\infty}.

Proof.

Since {Fk​(B)}k≥0\{F^{k}(B)\}_{k\geq 0} is a descending chain by Lemma 5.4, B∞B_{\infty} is the greatest lower bound of that chain. Similarly, X∞X_{\infty} is the greatest lower bound of the descending chain {Fk​([⊥,⊤])}k≥0\{F^{k}([\bot,\top])\}_{k\geq 0}. By monotonicity of FF (in the sound intervals, Lemma 5.7) and B⊆[⊥,⊤]B\subseteq[\bot,\top], we then have Fk​(B)⊆Fk​([⊥,⊤])F^{k}(B)\subseteq F^{k}([\bot,\top]) for all k≥0k\geq 0. Then for all k≥0k\geq 0, B∞⊆Fk​(B)⊆Fk​([⊥,⊤])B_{\infty}\subseteq F^{k}(B)\subseteq F^{k}([\bot,\top]). Then, B∞B_{\infty} is a lower bound of the chain {Fk​([⊥,⊤])}k≥0\{F^{k}([\bot,\top])\}_{k\geq 0}, so B∞⊆X∞B_{\infty}\subseteq X_{\infty}. ∎

These results have a useful consequence: we may begin our process at any interval, and applying the iterative refinement process will always take us to an interval that is at least as good as X∞X_{\infty}. Furthermore, if we begin at a sound interval, the iterative refinement process will end in a sound interval. This can be thought of as a soundness property of FF.

This allows us to interleave other methods and heuristics to forcibly shrink the bound (when possible). These heuristics can be thought of as a “jump-start” for FF, and the refinement process defined by FF can be thought of as a search space restriction for the heuristics. The jump-start is especially useful when the bound is stuck at a fixed point of FF. Recall that at each step of refinement, the upper and lower bounds of a sound interval always remain above and below the solutions previously contained. By forcibly pushing either the upper or the lower bound in such a way they no longer bound some solutions, but still bound at least one (to remain sound), we can effectively jump-start the refinement process so it is no longer stuck, and hope for a snowball effect where the bounds continue improving each other once again. This can be visually depicted in Figure 1(a), where [xℓ,xu][x^{\ell},x^{u}] is stuck since it must bound all solutions. In Figure 1(b), xℓx^{\ell} is forcibly advanced (using some heuristic or a domain-specific sound advancement), which enables xux^{u} to continue improving.

In the Section 6, we take advantage of this observation to create an effective algorithm for narrowing in on exact fixed points. It also makes note of a second useful observation: Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4 show that if Fk​(B)F^{k}(B) is not a valid interval or it is not a subset of BB, then it must be the case that BB is not sound. We will use this fact to prune the search space and maintain a more manageable set of search intervals.

5.1. An Abstract Interpretation for the Approximation

In many cases, computation of fBℓf^{\ell}_{B} and fBuf^{u}_{B} is very expensive. It may require enumeration over an exponentially sized lattice (in the size of the problem input). While the examples in this paper are centered around instances where these functions are relatively cheap to compute, we present a new theorem, to the best of our knowledge, that enables an abstraction for sound non-monotone fixed point approximations. In this section, we will let ≤p\leq_{p} be an ordering over pairs: (x1,y1)≤p(x2,y2)(x_{1},y_{1})\leq_{p}(x_{2},y_{2}) iff x2≤x1∧y1≤y2x_{2}\leq x_{1}\land y_{1}\leq y_{2}. This ordering represents the precision of an interval approximation. It is evident that for B1,B2∈𝔅B_{1},B_{2}\in\mathfrak{B} represented as pairs of the lower and upper bounds, B1≤pB2B_{1}\leq_{p}B_{2} iff B1⊆B2B_{1}\subseteq B_{2}. It can then be thought of as an extension of set inclusion to all pairs. We will think of 𝔅\mathfrak{B} as being a subset of L2L^{2} here.

We will refer to FfF_{f} as the function FF constructed before but parameterized by the function ff. Let CC and AA be complete lattices. Let αu,αℓ:C→A\alpha^{u},\alpha^{\ell}:C\to A and γu,γℓ:A→C\gamma^{u},\gamma^{\ell}:A\to C be monotone such that αu⊣γu\alpha^{u}\dashv\gamma^{u} and γℓ⊣αℓ\gamma^{\ell}\dashv\alpha^{\ell} are Galois insertions. We will also let, for any B=[xℓ,xu]∈C2B=[x^{\ell},x^{u}]\in C^{2}, α⁡(B)=[αℓ​(xℓ),αu​(xu)]∈A2\alpha(B)=[\alpha^{\ell}(x^{\ell}),\alpha^{u}(x^{u})]\in A^{2} (and similarly for γ\gamma). Note that, as shown in the proof of the following theorem, αℓ≤αu\alpha^{\ell}\leq\alpha^{u}.

Theorem 5.9.

Let f:C→Cf:C\to C and f♯,f♭:A→Af^{\sharp},f^{\flat}:A\to A satisfy

f♭∘αℓ≤Aαℓ∘fαu∘f≤Af♯∘αuf^{\flat}\circ\alpha^{\ell}\leq_{A}\alpha^{\ell}\circ f\qquad\alpha^{u}\circ f\leq_{A}f^{\sharp}\circ\alpha^{u}

and for all B∈A2B\in A^{2} let F♯:A2→A2F^{\sharp}:A^{2}\to A^{2} be defined by F♯​(B)=[lfpB⁡((f♭)Bℓ),gfpB⁡((f♯)Bu)]F^{\sharp}(B)=[\operatorname{lfp}_{B}((f^{\flat})^{\ell}_{B}),\operatorname{gfp}_{B}((f^{\sharp})^{u}_{B})]. Then for all B∈C2B\in C^{2},

α(F(B))≤pF♯(α(B)).\alpha(F(B))\leq_{p}F^{\sharp}(\alpha(B)).
Proof.

See appendix. ∎

This theorem gives a simple recipe for an abstract interpretation on the approximation operator FF. The only requirement is to have a such αℓ,γℓ\alpha^{\ell},\gamma^{\ell} and αu,γu\alpha^{u},\gamma^{u}. The first pair can be thought of as an under-approximating abstraction while the second pair can be thought of as an over-approximating abstraction (in the standard abstract interpretation sense). Then, we may use the best transformers f♭=αℓ​f​γℓf^{\flat}=\alpha^{\ell}f\gamma^{\ell} and f♯=αu​f​γuf^{\sharp}=\alpha^{u}f\gamma^{u}, which are known to satisfy the inequalities required by the theorem. It is not hard to see that these best correct approximations (in the Cousot sense (cousot1979)) also yield the best correct approximation F♯F^{\sharp} for FF.

Corollary 5.10.

If α⁡(F⁡(B))∈𝔅A\alpha(F(B))\in\mathfrak{B}^{A}, then F♯​(α⁡(B))∈𝔅AF^{\sharp}(\alpha(B))\in\mathfrak{B}^{A} α⁡(F⁡(B))⊆F♯​(α⁡(B))\alpha(F(B))\subseteq F^{\sharp}(\alpha(B)).

6. A Branch-and-Bound for Tightening Approximations

Thus far, the described iterative refinement process has been very safe: it progresses monotonically only to a provably sound bound at each step. As previously hinted, we now look at methods for speculatively advancing the bound rather than cautiously advancing. This is achieved using a branch-and-bound style algorithm that functions using iterative refinement and pruning when a bound is provably unsound. In the context of this algorithm, we will let I​R​(B)IR(B) be the repeated iteration of FF on BB. This can be any number of iterations, whether it is to a fixed point or not. The more iterations, the tighter the resulting bound (if BB is sound, by Lemma 5.4).

Refine

Suppose we have a set of sound bounds B​o​u​n​d​sBounds. For each B∈B​o​u​n​d​sB\in Bounds, let B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} be a decomposition of BB so that B=B1∪B2B=B_{1}\cup B_{2} and each BiB_{i} is a valid bound (Bi∈𝔅B_{i}\in\mathfrak{B}). Then, run the iterative refinement algorithm on each BiB_{i} to get I​R​(Bi)IR(B_{i}). By Lemma 5.3, all the fixed points that were contained in the intervals of B​o​u​n​d​sBounds are still contained after this operation.

Prune

Let I​R​(Bi)=[xℓ,xu]IR(B_{i})=[x^{\ell},x^{u}]. If xℓ≰xux^{\ell}\not\leq x^{u}, then by Lemma 5.3, it must be the case that there are no fixed points of ff contained in BiB_{i} (that is, BiB_{i} is not sound). Similarly, if I​R​(Bi)⊈BiIR(B_{i})\not\subseteq B_{i}, Lemma 5.4 proves that BiB_{i} is unsound. In these cases, we will prune BiB_{i} from the search space B​o​u​n​d​sBounds. Note that these conditions are sufficient to determine that BiB_{i} is not sound, but not necessary.

Merge

We then merge any “adjacent” bounds in the following sense: for any two bounds A1=[a1ℓ,a1u]∈𝔅,A2=[a2ℓ,a2u]∈𝔅A_{1}=[a_{1}^{\ell},a_{1}^{u}]\in\mathfrak{B},A_{2}=[a_{2}^{\ell},a_{2}^{u}]\in\mathfrak{B}, A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} are adjacent if A1∪A2∈𝔅A_{1}\cup A_{2}\in\mathfrak{B} (where ∪\cup is typical set union rather than a join of intervals). Finally, we update B​o​u​n​d​sBounds by joining all adjacent bounds (after pruning and iterative refinement), resulting in a set of refined, non-adjacent bounds.

After repeating this process to a fixed point (or stopping earlier), we end with a set of smaller bounds such that every fixed point μ\mu of ff is contained in some B∈B​o​u​n​d​sB\in Bounds. Observe that this algorithm utilizes the soundness theorems. An early-stopping technique can be added by checking if the endpoints of a bound is a fixed point after iterative refinement. In this case, we do not need to continue the search, and we can simply return the fixed point. If we are interested in all fixed points or in an optimal fixed point (by some norm), then we may store the discovered fixed point, update the current interval, and continue the search.

In Algorithm 1, we will let

ϕ⁡(B)≡I​R​(B)∈𝔅∧I​R​(B)⊆B\phi(B)\equiv IR(B)\in\mathfrak{B}\land IR(B)\subseteq B

If ¬ϕ⁡(B)\neg\phi(B), then Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4 prove that BB is not sound. If at any point during the I​RIR process, these conditions fail, then we may choose to stop it immediately to save time. We also use a procedure Decompose​(B)\textsc{Decompose}(B). Assume that for any B∈𝔅B\in\mathfrak{B}, Decompose​(B)\textsc{Decompose}(B) correctly returns a pair of adjacent non-trivial (when possible) bounds B1,B2∈𝔅B_{1},B_{2}\in\mathfrak{B} such that B1∪B2=BB_{1}\cup B_{2}=B. The if-statement’s guard on line 8 ensures that if BB is a singleton, then it will be finalized. We later show how such a procedure can easily be devised in the case of a lattice of subsets.

Lemma 6.1.

The following are invariants of the outer while loop in Algorithm 1:

  1. (1)

    B​o​u​n​d​s⊆𝔅Bounds\subseteq\mathfrak{B}.

  2. (2)

    ∀B∈B​o​u​n​d​s\forall B\in Bounds, B⊆BIB\subseteq B_{I}.

  3. (3)

    ∀B1,B2∈B​o​u​n​d​s\forall B_{1},B_{2}\in Bounds such that B1≠B2B_{1}\neq B_{2}, B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} are not adjacent.

Proof.

See appendix. ∎

Theorem 6.2.

If LL satisfies both ACC and DCC, Algorithm 1 terminates in a finite number of iterations.

Proof.

See appendix. ∎

Theorem 6.3.

The following invariant holds: for all μ∈Fix⁡(f)\mu\in\operatorname{Fix}(f) in BIB_{I}, there exists a bound B∈F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​sB\in Final\cup Bounds such that μ∈B\mu\in B.

Proof.

See appendix. ∎

Corollary 6.4.

Upon termination, all fixed points of ff are contained in at least one interval B∈F​i​n​a​lB\in Final.

Corollary 6.5.

If the intervals produced by Decompose are disjoint, then the invariant from Theorem 6.3 strengthens: for all fixed points μ∈BI\mu\in B_{I} of ff, there exists a unique B∈F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​sB\in Final\cup Bounds.

We substantiate the improved tightness of the resulting approximating bounds in two ways. The first is by observing that the proof of invariant (2) of Lemma 6.1 proves ∀B∈B​o​u​n​d​s\forall B\in Bounds, B⊆I​R​(BI)B\subseteq IR(B_{I}). The following theorem shows the second way, proving that the total size of the search space is no larger than the AFT best approximation I​R​(BI)IR(B_{I}). We use |⋅||\cdot| to mean set cardinality for interval sets as well.

Theorem 6.6.

Let S⁡(F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​s)=∑B∈F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​s|B|S(Final\cup Bounds)=\sum_{B\in Final\cup Bounds}|B|. Then, S⁡(F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​s)≤|I​R​(BI)|S(Final\cup Bounds)\leq|IR(B_{I})| is an invariant of the outer loop of Algorithm 1 if the intervals produced by Decompose are disjoint.

Proof.

This comes immediately from the fact that the bounds in F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​sFinal\cup Bounds are disjoint and contained in I​R​(BI)IR(B_{I}). Thus the size of the (set) union of the intervals in F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​sFinal\cup Bounds is equal to S⁡(F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​s)S(Final\cup Bounds), and the union is a subset of I​R​(BI)IR(B_{I}), so S⁡(F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​s)≤|I​R​(BI)|S(Final\cup Bounds)\leq|IR(B_{I})|. ∎

To illustrate an implementation of Decompose whose produced sub-intervals are disjoint, let L=2SL=2^{S} for some set SS ordered by subset inclusion. Then, if [A,B]∈𝔅[A,B]\in\mathfrak{B} (with non-zero height), arbitrarily choose x∈B∖Ax\in B\setminus A. It is evident that [A,B∖{a}][A,B\setminus\{a\}] and [A∪{a},B][A\cup\{a\},B] are adjacent and disjoint. Observe that the effectiveness of Algorithm 1 can be dependent on the implementation of Decompose. If the decomposition happens to be good (in the sense that it enables the iterative refinement to greatly reduce the decomposed bounds), then the algorithm will be very effective. One may decide to implement a context-aware version of Decompose that can learn from decompositions that did not previously work. This would require not finalizing refined bounds that join back to their parent bound.

As it stands, the proof of Theorem 6.2 tells us that the outer loop runs for at most ℓ⁡(BI)\ell(B_{I}) iterations. In the case of 2S2^{S}, this states that it runs for at most |S||S| iterations. The issue is that |B​o​u​n​d​s||Bounds| may be exponentially large, so the inner loop can take exponential time. To remedy this, we consider a budget condition modification for bounding |B​o​u​n​d​s||Bounds| to polynomial size. For bounds B1=[x1ℓ,x1u]∈𝔅B_{1}=[x^{\ell}_{1},x^{u}_{1}]\in\mathfrak{B} and B2=[x2ℓ,x2u]∈BB_{2}=[x^{\ell}_{2},x^{u}_{2}]\in B, we will let hull⁡(B1,B2)=[x1ℓ⊓x2ℓ,x1u⊔x2u]\operatorname{hull}(B_{1},B_{2})=[x^{\ell}_{1}\sqcap x^{\ell}_{2},x^{u}_{1}\sqcup x^{u}_{2}] (a join under the precision ordering).

Budget Condition

We can modify Algorithm 1 as follows: let n=ℓ⁡(BI)n=\ell(B_{I}) and K=poly⁡(n)K=\operatorname{poly}(n) (and non-zero). Whenever a bound is added to N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds and |N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​s|>K|NewBounds|>K, choose a pair B1,B2∈N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sB_{1},B_{2}\in NewBounds that minimizes

|hull⁡(B1,B2)|−(|B1|+|B2|)|\operatorname{hull}(B_{1},B_{2})|-(|B_{1}|+|B_{2}|)

and replace B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} with hull⁡(B1,B2)\operatorname{hull}(B_{1},B_{2}). Note that pruning its subsets is not necessary since if hull⁡(B1,B2)\operatorname{hull}(B_{1},B_{2}) is added and there exists C⊆hull⁡(B1,B2)C\subseteq\operatorname{hull}(B_{1},B_{2}), then either B1,CB_{1},C or B2,CB_{2},C would have been chosen to minimize the delta instead. This heuristic keeps the cumulative size of the intervals as small as possible while bounding |B​o​u​n​d​s||Bounds| to polynomial size. With this budget condition, we may safely assume that |B​o​u​n​d​s|≤K|Bounds|\leq K is invariant. Observe that adding this condition breaks the guarantee of termination, even with finite height lattices. By Theorem 6.3, we can choose to stop at any point while maintaining soundness (in F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​sFinal\cup Bounds). We will let TT be a chosen number of iterations to perform before forcibly terminating. This modification upholds the invariant of Theorem 6.3, and is forced to terminate in finite time given that I​RIR terminates in finite time. This is described by the following theorem and the discussion that follows.

Theorem 6.7.

With the budget condition, the number of I​RIR calls in Algorithm 1 is no greater than 2​K​T+1=poly⁡(n)⋅T2KT+1=\operatorname{poly}(n)\cdot T.

Proof.

The budget condition guarantees that |B​o​u​n​d​s|≤K|Bounds|\leq K is invariant. The only time I​RIR is called is (1) at initialization, and (2) in the inner loop. Initialization contributes one I​RIR call, and each iteration of the inner loop contributes at most 22 calls. Since |B​o​u​n​d​s|≤K|Bounds|\leq K, the inner loop performs at most KK iterations, so the inner loop contributes at most 2​K2K calls. Finally, since the outer loop iterates no more than TT times, it contributes no more than 2​K​T2KT times, so there are a total of 2​K​T+12KT+1 calls to I​RIR. ∎

This theorem shows that, the budget condition modification, if a call to I​RIR takes poly⁡(n)\operatorname{poly}(n) time (whether by structural properties of ff, lattice abstractions, or restricted iterations of FF), Algorithm 1 takes poly⁡(n)⋅T\operatorname{poly}(n)\cdot T time. This makes note of the fact that choosing a B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} to replace by their hull is a polynomial operation in KK (and thus in nn). Additionally, if TT is chosen to be poly⁡(n)\operatorname{poly}(n), then the algorithm takes poly⁡(n)\operatorname{poly}(n) time. The trade off is that the produced bounds will be larger and Theorem 6.6 may not always hold. This trade off is, in most cases, worth it (as is later illustrated).

6.1. An Example With Answer Set Programming

Consider the problem of finding a minimum size stable model for a logic program PP. By definition, the stable models are exactly the subsets MM of the Herbrand base of PP such that M=SP​(M)M=S_{P}(M). It was already established that SPS_{P} is not monotone, but rather it is anti-monotone. In this section, we will see how anti-monotonicity makes approximating the fixed points of SPS_{P} an easy computation, and demonstrate an application of Algorithm 1 on a simple non-stratified logic program.

For k≥1k\geq 1, let (SP)kℓ,(SP)ku(S_{P})_{k}^{\ell},(S_{P})_{k}^{u} be the resulting envelopes after kk applications of FF with the function SPS_{P}, and let Fk​([∅,HP])=[xkℓ,xku]F^{k}([\emptyset,H_{P}])=[x_{k}^{\ell},x_{k}^{u}].

(SP)kℓ​(M)\displaystyle(S_{P})_{k}^{\ell}(M) =infM⊆A⊆xk−1uSP​(A)=SP​(xk−1u)\displaystyle=\inf_{M\subseteq A\subseteq x_{k-1}^{u}}S_{P}(A)=S_{P}(x_{k-1}^{u})
(SP)ku​(M)\displaystyle(S_{P})_{k}^{u}(M) =supxk−1ℓ⊆A⊆MSP​(A)=SP​(xk−1ℓ)\displaystyle=\sup_{x_{k-1}^{\ell}\subseteq A\subseteq M}S_{P}(A)=S_{P}(x_{k-1}^{\ell})

by anti-monotonicity of SP​(A)S_{P}(A). Thus, computing each of the approximating functions is a matter of a single application of SPS_{P}. Furthermore, since (SP)kℓ(S_{P})_{k}^{\ell} and (SP)ku(S_{P})_{k}^{u} are constant functions, their lfp/gfp-equivalent functions admit a single known fixed point. Thus computing lfpB⁡((SP)kℓ)\operatorname{lfp}_{B}((S_{P})_{k}^{\ell}) and gfpB⁡((SP)ku)\operatorname{gfp}_{B}((S_{P})_{k}^{u}) requires only a single application of SPS_{P} for each, which is an easy computation. Specifically, for k>0k>0

lfpB⁡((SP)kℓ)\displaystyle\operatorname{lfp}_{B}((S_{P})_{k}^{\ell}) =xk−1ℓ∪SP​(xk−1u)\displaystyle=x_{k-1}^{\ell}\cup S_{P}(x_{k-1}^{u})
gfpB⁡((SP)ku)\displaystyle\operatorname{gfp}_{B}((S_{P})_{k}^{u}) =xk−1u∩SP​(xk−1ℓ)\displaystyle=x_{k-1}^{u}\cap S_{P}(x_{k-1}^{\ell})

This approximation of the stable models is equivalently presented as an example in (denecker2004). We will show that Algorithm 1 can be used to narrow in on the exact stable models by taking advantage of a known fixed point theorem for anti-monotone functions.

For an anti-monotone function ff, if μ\mu is the least fixed point of the monotone function f2f^{2}, then μ\mu and ν=f⁡(μ)\nu=f(\mu) are the dual fixed points (sometimes called the extreme oscillating pair) of ff where f⁡(ν)=μf(\nu)=\mu and f⁡(μ)=νf(\mu)=\nu (gelder1993). Furthermore, μ\mu is a lower bound for the fixed points of ff and ν\nu is an upper bound for the fixed points of ff.

It is not hard to see that the iterative refinement process I​RIR for an anti-monotone function beginning at [⊥,⊤][\bot,\top] converges (in a finite height lattice) at the bound [μ,ν][\mu,\nu], and thus in the case of SPS_{P}, the converged upper bound is a set of atoms that are true in some stable model of PP and the converged lower bound is a set of atoms that is true in all stable models of PP (relating to the well-founded semantics). That is, the lower bound is certain and the upper bound is possible among the stable models.

We will now illustrate this with an example non-stratified logic program PP.

p\displaystyle p ←¬qr←p\displaystyle\leftarrow\neg q\qquad r\leftarrow p
q\displaystyle q ←¬ps←q\displaystyle\leftarrow\neg p\qquad s\leftarrow q

Note that the stable models of PP are {p,r}\{p,r\} and {q,s}\{q,s\}. Their intersection is empty and their union is the full Herbrand base, so we expect the iterative refinement to get stuck at this unimproved interval. We begin with the bounds x0ℓ=∅x_{0}^{\ell}=\emptyset and x0u=HPx_{0}^{u}=H_{P} (the Herbrand base of PP). Then as derived earlier,

x1ℓ\displaystyle x_{1}^{\ell} =SP​(x0u)=∅\displaystyle=S_{P}(x_{0}^{u})=\emptyset
x1u\displaystyle x_{1}^{u} =SP​(x0ℓ)=HP\displaystyle=S_{P}(x_{0}^{\ell})=H_{P}

and indeed, [x1ℓ,x1u][x_{1}^{\ell},x_{1}^{u}] (the AFT canonical best approximation) is stuck bounding the entire space. To close in on the stable models, we apply Algorithm 1 with the input bound HPH_{P}. As already shown, I​R​(HP)=[∅,HP]IR(H_{P})=[\emptyset,H_{P}]. Now this bound will be decomposed. To do so, we may use the method for set lattices described earlier. We first choose an arbitrary element in HP∖∅H_{P}\setminus\emptyset, say pp, and split the interval into B1=[∅,HP∖{p}]B_{1}=[\emptyset,H_{P}\setminus\{p\}] and B2=[∅∪{p},HP]B_{2}=[\emptyset\cup\{p\},H_{P}]. Then we apply iterative refinement on each of these bounds, beginning with the first:

F⁡([∅,HP∖{p}])=[{q,s},{q,r,s}]F([\emptyset,H_{P}\setminus\{p\}])=[\{q,s\},\{q,r,s\}]

so ϕ⁡(B1)\phi(B_{1}) holds and I​R​(B1)IR(B_{1}) is kept. For I​R​(B2)IR(B_{2}), we observe:

F⁡([{p},HP])=[{p},{p,r}]F([\{p\},H_{P}])=[\{p\},\{p,r\}]

and at this point, it is evident that these bounds will be split to singletons and the algorithm will terminate. Discarding the singleton intervals before finalizing that do not have a stable model leaves us with {p,r}\{p,r\} and {q,s}\{q,s\}, the exact stable models.

7. Application to Speculative Program Analyses

Finally, we have reached a point where all prior algorithms, results, and examples can work together in an application to a speculative program analysis. The problem faced in this section, when observed from a certain angle, reflects the kind of reasoning seen in stable model semantics. A standard program analysis works by soundly approximating the program state, whereas a speculative program analysis may make potentially incorrect assumptions about the program in an attempt to improve either precision or speed, and may need to retract assumptions if they are proven unsound by the analysis. A set of assumptions are stable if they reach a fixed point in the program analysis. That is, under a stable set of assumptions σ\sigma, the least fixed point of the forward abstract transfer function under the assumptions of σ\sigma does not disprove σ\sigma. With this framing, the parallelism to stable model semantics becomes more evident. Since they share the same flavor, we will see that the applicability of the earlier methods also apply nicely here.

Let PP be a program with (concrete) collecting semantics 𝒮\mathcal{S} and a monotone, Scott-continuous forward transformer FP:𝒮→𝒮F_{P}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{S}. Let (D,⊑)(D,\sqsubseteq) be a complete lattice and α⊣γ\alpha\dashv\gamma be a Galois connection between 𝒮\mathcal{S} and DD. In a typical fashion, let FP♯:D→DF_{P}^{\sharp}:D\to D be the standard sound abstract transfer function (that is both monotone and Scott-continuous). We will assume a finite set 𝒜\mathcal{A} of speculations that will encode assertions about program states. For instance, an element in 𝒜\mathcal{A} may encode the assertion “at location ℓ\ell, y>0y>0.” Given an assertion a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, we let Πa:D→D\Pi_{a}:D\to D be an abstract projector that strengthens a given abstract state using the assumption that aa is true. We may reasonably require Πa\Pi_{a} to be monotone (if S1♯⊑S2♯S^{\sharp}_{1}\sqsubseteq S_{2}^{\sharp}, then applying the same strengthening to both preserves the ordering), reductive (Πa​(S♯)⊑S♯\Pi_{a}(S^{\sharp})\sqsubseteq S^{\sharp}), and idempotent (Πa​(Πa​(S♯))=Πa​(S♯)\Pi_{a}(\Pi_{a}(S^{\sharp}))=\Pi_{a}(S^{\sharp})). For a set of assertions σ⊆𝒜\sigma\subseteq\mathcal{A}, we conveniently let Πσ\Pi_{\sigma} be the pointwise meet of the abstract projectors {Πa∣a∈σ}\{\Pi_{a}\mid a\in\sigma\}.

We also let for a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, 𝐨𝐤a:D→{true,false,unknown}\mathbf{ok}_{a}:D\to\{\textbf{true},\textbf{false},\textbf{unknown}\} be a function that determines aa’s compatibility with the given abstract state. In the case of static analyses, this may be defined by

𝐨𝐤a​(S♯)={falseif S♯ entails ¬atrueif S♯ proves aunknownotherwise\mathbf{ok}_{a}(S^{\sharp})=\begin{cases}\textbf{false}&\text{if $S^{\sharp}$ entails $\neg a$}\\ \textbf{true}&\text{if $S^{\sharp}$ proves $a$}\\ \textbf{unknown}&\text{otherwise}\\ \end{cases}

In a dynamic analysis, this may be defined by 𝐨𝐤a​(S♯)=false\mathbf{ok}_{a}(S^{\sharp})=\textbf{false} if any runtime counter-example has occurred, and unknown otherwise (in general a two-valued definition determining whether or not a counterexample has been seen). For any set of assertions σ⊆𝒜\sigma\subseteq\mathcal{A}, the σ\sigma-constrained abstract transformer is

FP,σ♯=Πσ∘FP♯F^{\sharp}_{P,\sigma}=\Pi_{\sigma}\circ F^{\sharp}_{P}

and FP,σ♯F^{\sharp}_{P,\sigma} is monotone and Scott-continuous for any fixed σ\sigma. Observe that FP,σ♯F^{\sharp}_{P,\sigma} is anti-monotone in σ\sigma (a smaller set of assertions leads to a larger abstract state in the precision ordering). For fixed σ\sigma, the standard abstract analysis gives

A⁡(σ)=lfp⁡(FP,σ♯)A(\sigma)=\operatorname{lfp}(F^{\sharp}_{P,\sigma})

To extract a set of valid assumptions, we first define the set Safe⁡(S♯)={a∈𝒜∣𝐨𝐤a​(S♯)≠false}\mathrm{Safe}(S^{\sharp})=\{a\in\mathcal{A}\mid\mathbf{ok}_{a}(S^{\sharp})\neq\textbf{false}\}. That is, Safe⁡(S♯)\mathrm{Safe}(S^{\sharp}) is the set of assumptions that are “safe to keep for now” (those that the abstraction can’t refute). This definition can be adjusted to only keep self-justified assumptions by instead taking the assertions a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} where 𝐨𝐤a​(S♯)=true\mathbf{ok}_{a}(S^{\sharp})=\textbf{true}. Finally, an operator for updating the current set of assumptions σ\sigma can be defined as

Φ⁡(σ)=Safe⁡(A⁡(σ))\Phi(\sigma)=\mathrm{Safe}(A(\sigma))

An intuition for this operator is that we begin with a set of assumptions σ\sigma, analyze the program under these assumptions, and then retract any such speculations that are falsified by A⁡(σ)A(\sigma). Furthermore, the stable sets of assumptions are exactly the fixed points of Φ\Phi, since σ=Φ⁡(σ)\sigma=\Phi(\sigma) is precisely consistent with the speculative analysis A⁡(σ)A(\sigma).

Lemma 7.1.

Safe:D→2𝒜\mathrm{Safe}:D\to 2^{\mathcal{A}} is monotone.

Proof.

Let S1♯⊑S2♯S^{\sharp}_{1}\sqsubseteq S^{\sharp}_{2}, and let Refa​(S♯)≡𝐨𝐤a​(S♯)=false\mathrm{Ref}_{a}(S^{\sharp})\equiv\mathbf{ok}_{a}(S^{\sharp})=\textbf{false} be a predicate that is true iff assertion aa is refuted by S♯S^{\sharp}. Then, Refa​(S2♯)⇒Refa​(S1♯)\mathrm{Ref}_{a}(S^{\sharp}_{2})\Rightarrow\mathrm{Ref}_{a}(S^{\sharp}_{1}) since a more precise abstract state can refute more assertions. Then taking complements in 2𝒜2^{\mathcal{A}} gives Safe⁡(S1♯)⊆Safe⁡(S2♯)\mathrm{Safe}(S^{\sharp}_{1})\subseteq\mathrm{Safe}(S^{\sharp}_{2}). ∎

From this lemma and the anti-monotonicity of AA (due to the anti-monotonicity of FP,σ♯F^{\sharp}_{P,\sigma} w.r.t. σ\sigma), the operator Φ\Phi is anti-monotone. As shown in the previous section, this simplifies the iterative refinement to alternative fixed point iteration of an anti-monotone function, promoting computational efficiency. By keeping track of the analysis results throughout an application of Algorithm 1, it terminates with the stable sets of assumptions (either exact or approximating bounds) along with their resulting analysis. This can be beneficial for choosing an analysis that maximizes an objective such as precision (which in the case of precision, must be maximized by at least one of Φ\Phi’s fixed points). In the particular case of dynamic analyses, counter-examples may arrive in an online fashion. If such a counter-example arrives for the current set of (previously stable) assumptions, it would be useful to have a more conservative fixed point (stable set of assumptions) to fall back on. The DMT operator alone is also useful (and cheaper to compute) in this case, since the resulting lower bound will be a set of safe assumptions that appear in every stable set of assertions. The upper bound will then be a set of assumptions that are safe in some stable set of assertions. This approximation, as discussed earlier, may be coarse, in which case it can be fed to Algorithm 1 for improvement.

The issue with Algorithm 1 in this application is that it requires running many analyses, which can be simply infeasible for large programs. To achieve speed-ups in this regard, memoizing basic transfer results FP♯​(⋅)F^{\sharp}_{P}(\cdot) and reusing them in future computations of AA avoids lots of redundant computation. A lazy evaluation may then be done: if A⁡(σ)A(\sigma) has been computed and we need A⁡(σ′)A(\sigma^{\prime}) where σ⊆σ′\sigma\subseteq\sigma^{\prime}, simply take the results of A⁡(σ)A(\sigma) and revisit only nodes affected by σ′∖σ\sigma^{\prime}\setminus\sigma (and if σ′⊆σ\sigma^{\prime}\subseteq\sigma, the same lazy evaluation can be done by revisiting only nodes affected by retracting σ∖σ′\sigma\setminus\sigma^{\prime}). Since most nodes won’t be affected by one assertion (they are typically targeted to one small part of the program), this lazy evaluation will be fast and Algorithm 1 will become feasible to compute. The exact details of such a lazy evaluation are outside the scope of this paper.

In the case of optimistic hybrid analyses (devecsery2018), we likely care more about the speed and resource usage of the dynamic analysis than the static one. In this case, finding stable sets of assumptions for the static analyzer does not affect the speed of the dynamic analysis. In fact, instead of sampling many executions to find likely invariants as prescribed in (devecsery2018), this technique can instead be used to find the likely invariants in a more predictable way with guarantees.

Theorem 7.2.

All stable sets of assumptions σ⊆𝒜\sigma\subseteq\mathcal{A} are contained in some interval in F​i​n​a​lFinal upon termination of Algorithm 1.

As a final note, we consider the relationship between a stable set of assumptions σ\sigma and its corresponding analysis A⁡(σ)A(\sigma), and how it can be changed. In a similar fashion as the assume-guarantee paradigm, A⁡(σ)A(\sigma) is not necessarily sound with respect to the concrete program, but rather it is sound conditional on σ\sigma. That is, the result is valid provided the speculations hold. If we instead define Safe∀​(S♯)={a∈𝒜∣𝐨𝐤a​(S♯)=true}\mathrm{Safe}_{\forall}(S^{\sharp})=\{a\in\mathcal{A}\mid\mathbf{ok}_{a}(S^{\sharp})=\textbf{true}\} and Φ⁡(σ)=Safe∀​(A⁡(σ))\Phi(\sigma)=\mathrm{Safe}_{\forall}(A(\sigma)), then its fixed points contain only assumptions that have been proven by the abstract facts. Then, Πσ\Pi_{\sigma} only removes unreachable states, yielding α∘FP⊑Πσ∘FP♯∘α=FP,σ♯∘α\alpha\circ F_{P}\sqsubseteq\Pi_{\sigma}\circ F^{\sharp}_{P}\circ\alpha=F^{\sharp}_{P,\sigma}\circ\alpha. Thus with this definition of Φ\Phi, the analysis is sound.

Given the circumstances, either an unsound or a sound analysis may be suitable. For example, the previously mentioned optimistic hybrid analysis takes advantage of the extra precision provided by unsound analyses (in hopes that it is validated). However, in a purely static setting unsoundness can lead to incorrect optimizations.

8. Application as a Pre-Processing Step

Theorems 6.3 and 6.6 are helpful for two reasons: (1) the final result provides a smaller search space containing the fixed points, which can be used in pre-processing, and (2) it shows that the algorithm is anytime (and I​R​(⋅)IR(\cdot) is, by its definition, anytime), so it can be interrupted to have minimal impact on the total computation time. To illustrate this, we describe how it can be implemented as a pre-processing step for an ASP solver. There are a couple ways to do this.

First, suppose we have a bound [A,B][A,B] on some stable models. One method is to partially evaluate the program using AA and BB by substituting true for atoms in AA and false for atoms not in BB since all atoms in AA are in the stable models in [A,B][A,B], and all atoms not in BB are not in those stable models. Then, simply drop the rules whose bodies become false, remove satisfied body literals, and simplify constraints/aggregates. This yields a much smaller, easier to compute program that an ASP solver can very quickly process. Having bounds on the stable models (like what is achieved by Algorithm 1) can then significantly reduce the workload of an ASP solver.

This is illustrated in the example from Figures 2 and 3. Figure 2 is the input logic program, and Figure 3 is its partial evaluation where the lower bound AA has atoms r​e​d​(1)red(1) and g​r​e​e​n​(4)green(4) and the upper bound BB does not contain the atom b​l​u​e​(2)blue(2). While the partially evaluated program looks syntactically larger, its grounded program (the program resulting from grounding all variables) is much smaller than the original program, as expected.

On the other hand, most ASP solvers support assumptions (as unit literals), which eliminates the need for the overhead of partially evaluating the program. Simply assume aa for all a∈Aa\in A and ¬x\neg x for all x∉Bx\notin B. Partial evaluation done manually still has its merits though: suppose we have bounds [A,B][A,B] and [A′,B′][A^{\prime},B^{\prime}] where A⊆A′A\subseteq A^{\prime} (or similarly in the case B′⊆BB^{\prime}\subseteq B). Then, instead of feeding the ASP solver the assumptions from AA and then separately feeding the assumptions from A′A^{\prime}, we may partially evaluate the program by setting AA to true, and then store the partial evaluation PA′P^{\prime}_{A}. Then, we may later perform a partial evaluation on PA′P^{\prime}_{A} setting the atoms A′∖AA^{\prime}\setminus A to true. This compositional evaluation removes lots of redundant computation.

That being said, Theorem 6.3 gives that all the bounds in F​i​n​a​l∪B​o​u​n​d​sFinal\cup Bounds at any point contain all the fixed points, and we also know that these bounds are non-adjacent. These bounds can then be used as described earlier to speed up the computation of the ASP solver. This is seen in the diagram depicted in Figure 4. Theorem 6.7 guarantees that applying the budget condition modification to Algorithm 1 restricts |B​o​u​n​d​s||Bounds| to poly⁡(n)\operatorname{poly}(n), thus refraining the process from making exponentially many calls to the ASP solver.

9. Conclusion

We present an AFT-oriented paradigm for modeling stability in non-monotonic processes for PL algorithms that utilize backtracking, revision, and other kinds of non-monotonic behavior. To solve these non-monotone fixed point problems in practical industrial settings, we (1) provide an abstract interpretation for the fixed point approximations, (2) relax a known AFT operator and propose an anytime branch-and-bound algorithm that takes advantage of its structural properties for pruning, and (3) show that it achieves tighter bounds than those guaranteed in AFT. We demonstrate the applicability of these methods for speculative program analysis and ASP, where we also describe its effectiveness at pre-processing for such problems.

Proof of Lemma 6.1

Proof.

(1) Upon entering the outer loop, B​o​u​n​d​sBounds is a singleton set {I​R​(BI)}\{IR(B_{I})\} which is in 𝔅\mathfrak{B} (and sound) by Lemma 5.3 since BIB_{I} is sound. Inside the loop, the only line where B​o​u​n​d​sBounds is updated is line 22, where it is set to N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds. The only line where N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds is updated is line 19, where it adds the elements of K​e​e​pKeep, which contains either one or two elements. If K​e​e​pKeep contains only one element, then it is either the union of two adjacent intervals I​R​(B1),I​R​(B2)IR(B_{1}),IR(B_{2}) or it is I​R​(Bi)IR(B_{i}) for either B1B_{1} or B2B_{2}. In the former case, it must be the case that I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2)∈𝔅IR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2})\in\mathfrak{B} by definition of adjacency. In the latter case, ϕ⁡(Bi)\phi(B_{i}) must be true, so I​R​(Bi)∈𝔅IR(B_{i})\in\mathfrak{B}. In the case that K​e​e​pKeep contains two elements, then they must be I​R​(B1)IR(B_{1}) and I​R​(B2)IR(B_{2}), and they are not adjacent. Furthermore, it must be the case that ϕ⁡(B1)\phi(B_{1}) and ϕ⁡(B2)\phi(B_{2}) are true, so I​R​(B1),I​R​(B2)∈𝔅IR(B_{1}),IR(B_{2})\in\mathfrak{B}. Thus, N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds only contains elements in 𝔅\mathfrak{B}, and the invariant is true at the end of each loop. Upon exiting the loop, B​o​u​n​d​s=∅Bounds=\emptyset, so the statement is trivial.

(2) This statement initially holds since I​R​(BI)⊆BIIR(B_{I})\subseteq B_{I} by Lemma 5.4. We now look at N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds to see that the statement holds for it. At line 19, K​e​e​pKeep is either the union of two adjacent bounds I​R​(B1)IR(B_{1}) and I​R​(B2)IR(B_{2}), or it contains one or two sets I​R​(Bi)IR(B_{i}). In the former case, the invariant inductively tells us that B⊆BIB\subseteq B_{I}, so by correctness of Decompose, B1,B2⊆BB_{1},B_{2}\subseteq B, and by ϕ⁡(Bi)\phi(B_{i}), I​R​(Bi)⊆BiIR(B_{i})\subseteq B_{i}. Thus, I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2)⊆B1∪B2⊆B⊆BIIR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2})\subseteq B_{1}\cup B_{2}\subseteq B\subseteq B_{I}. In the latter case, ϕ⁡(Bi)\phi(B_{i}) gives that I​R​(Bi)⊆Bi⊆B⊆BIIR(B_{i})\subseteq B_{i}\subseteq B\subseteq B_{I}. Line 22 is the only time that B​o​u​n​d​sBounds is updated in this loop, and it is set to N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds, so the invariant is maintained at the end of each iteration for B​o​u​n​d​sBounds. Upon exiting the loop, the statement is trivially true since B​o​u​n​d​s=∅Bounds=\emptyset.

(3) The statement is vacuously true initially (B​o​u​n​d​sBounds does not contain any pair of distinct bounds). At line 19, it is guaranteed that the intervals in K​e​e​pKeep are non-adjacent by the if-statement’s guard on line 13. If they were adjacent prior that if-statement, they would be joined into a new interval I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2)⊆BIR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2})\subseteq B, and since BB is non-adjacent with all other bounds in B​o​u​n​d​sBounds, the same holds for I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2)IR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2}). It is then evident that all intervals in N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds are non-adjacent. Thus, since B​o​u​n​d​sBounds is set to N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds at line 22, the invariant is maintained at the end of each iteration of the outer loop. Upon exiting the outer loop, the statement is vacuously true. ∎

Proof of Theorem 6.2

Proof.

First note that since LL satisfies ACC and DCC, ℓ⁡(B)\ell(B) is defined for every B∈𝔅B\in\mathfrak{B} and {Fk​(B)}\{F^{k}(B)\} is guaranteed to stabilize at some k′k^{\prime} (and thus any instantiation of I​RIR terminates). We prove termination by showing that

π⁡(B​o​u​n​d​s)=maxB∈B​o​u​n​d​s⁡ℓ⁡(B)\pi(Bounds)=\max_{B\in Bounds}\ell(B)

strictly decreases at each iteration, and the while loop terminates after π⁡(B​o​u​n​d​s)=0\pi(Bounds)=0.

Consider a loop of the for loop beginning on line 6. First observe that at line 12, ℓ⁡(B)>0\ell(B)>0 ℓ⁡(B1),ℓ⁡(B2)<ℓ⁡(B)\ell(B_{1}),\ell(B_{2})<\ell(B) since if that were not the case then the guard of the if-statement on line 8 would be true (by interval properties, since any sub-interval with the same height or greater of the entire interval must be the entire interval), and the iteration would be skipped (by correctness of Decompose). After line 12,

π⁡(K​e​e​p)=max⁡{ℓ⁡(I​R​(Bi))∣i∈{1,2}∧ϕ⁡(Bi)}≤max⁡{ℓ⁡(Bi)∣i∈{1,2}∧ϕ⁡(Bi)}<ℓ⁡(B)\pi(Keep)=\max\{\ell(IR(B_{i}))\mid i\in\{1,2\}\wedge\phi(B_{i})\}\leq\max\{\ell(B_{i})\mid i\in\{1,2\}\wedge\phi(B_{i})\}<\ell(B)

If I​R​(B1)IR(B_{1}) and I​R​(B2)IR(B_{2}) are adjacent (assuming they are both added) and I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2)=BIR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2})=B, then line 17 is taken and BB is not added back to B​o​u​n​d​sBounds. We can say that BB contributed −ℓ⁡(B)-\ell(B) to the next iteration. If I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2)≠BIR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2})\neq B, then it is still a strict subset, so ℓ⁡(I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2))<ℓ⁡(B)\ell(IR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2}))<\ell(B), and BB is effectively replaced by I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2)IR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2}). We say that BB contributed ℓ⁡(I​R​(B1)∪I​R​(B2))−ℓ⁡(B)<0\ell(IR(B_{1})\cup IR(B_{2}))-\ell(B)<0 to the next iteration in this case. If I​R​(B1)IR(B_{1}) and I​R​(B2)IR(B_{2}) are not adjacent, then BB is replaced by both of them. Since their heights are strictly smaller than BB’s, we say that BB contributed π⁡(K​e​e​p)−ℓ⁡(B)<0\pi(Keep)-\ell(B)<0 to the next iteration. If, w.l.o.g., only I​R​(B1)IR(B_{1}) was kept, then BB contributed ℓ⁡(B1)−ℓ⁡(B)<0\ell(B_{1})-\ell(B)<0 to the next iteration. In all cases, BB contributed negative to the next iteration, and it is clear to see that since this is the case for each B∈B​o​u​n​d​sB\in Bounds, the max of B​o​u​n​d​sBounds must strictly decrease.

If π⁡(B​o​u​n​d​s)=0\pi(Bounds)=0, then either B​o​u​n​d​s=∅Bounds=\emptyset, in which case the loop terminates, or ∀B∈B​o​u​n​d​s\forall B\in Bounds, ℓ⁡(B)=0\ell(B)=0, in which case they will all be removed from B​o​u​n​d​sBounds as a result of the if-statement on line 8. On the next iteration, it will then necessarily be the case that B​o​u​n​d​s=∅Bounds=\emptyset and the loop terminates. ∎

Proof of Theorem 6.3

Proof.

Let μ∈Fix⁡(f)\mu\in\operatorname{Fix}(f) and μ∈BI\mu\in B_{I}. Then BI∈𝔅s​o​u​n​dB_{I}\in\mathfrak{B}_{sound} and by the proof of Lemma 5.3, μ∈I​R​(BI)\mu\in IR(B_{I}). Upon entering the loop, B​o​u​n​d​s={I​R​(BI)}Bounds=\{IR(B_{I})\}, so the invariant is initially true.

Now inductively let μ\mu be a fixed point of ff contained in some bound BB of B​o​u​n​d​sBounds (if there are none, then all fixed points are in F​i​n​a​lFinal inductively by the invariant). Then, by correctness of Decompose, μ∈B1\mu\in B_{1} or μ∈B2\mu\in B_{2} after line 7. Assume w.l.o.g. that μ∈B1\mu\in B_{1}. If line 9 is reached, then it must be the case that B1=BB_{1}=B, so after line 9 μ\mu will be in a bound in F​i​n​a​lFinal since μ∈B\mu\in B. If line 9 is not reached, then after line 12 we have that I​R​(B1)∈K​e​e​pIR(B_{1})\in Keep since B1B_{1} is sound (so ϕ⁡(B1)\phi(B_{1})). By the proof of Lemma 5.3, we have that μ∈I​R​(B1)\mu\in IR(B_{1}). By the if-else statement on line 16, either ⋃K​e​e​p\bigcup Keep is added to F​i​n​a​lFinal, in which case μ\mu is now in a bound in F​i​n​a​lFinal, or K​e​e​pKeep is added to N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds, in which case μ\mu is now in a bound in N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds. At line 22, B​o​u​n​d​sBounds is set to N​e​w​B​o​u​n​d​sNewBounds, so μ\mu would then be in a bound in B​o​u​n​d​sBounds by the end of the iteration. Thus the invariant holds at the end of each iteration.

Upon exiting the loop, the invariant is still upheld and B​o​u​n​d​s=∅Bounds=\emptyset so all fixed points are contained in a bound in F​i​n​a​lFinal. ∎
